summary.text: The proof’s core is a strengthened Jacobsthal-type congruence for \(\binom{Ap}{Bp}\), obtained by separating multiples of \(p\) in factorials, expanding the remaining product, and showing its first two correction terms have extra \(p\)-divisibility because the sums of \(x^{-1}\) and \(x^{-2}\) over units modulo powers of \(p\) vanish (with a reflection pairing supplying the second-order bound). The multinomial sum at \(mp\) is then split according to whether both lower indices are divisible by \(p\): the other terms vanish by valuation bounds, while the divisible terms reduce termwise to the sum at \(m\) using the binomial congruence and Kummer-type estimates; taking \(m=np^{k-1}\) gives the required exponent.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(N)=\sum_{r=0}^{N}\sum_{s=0}^{N-r}
 \left(\binom Nr\binom{N-r}{s}\right)^3.
\]
This is A141057: if the three blocks of an Abelian cube have common multiplicities \((r,s,N-r-s)\), then each block can be chosen in
\[
\frac{N!}{r!s!(N-r-s)!}=\binom Nr\binom{N-r}{s}
\]
ways, independently for the three blocks. Summing the cube of this multinomial coefficient over all multiplicity triples gives the displayed formula.

We prove that, for every prime \(p\geq 5\), every \(k\geq1\), and every \(n\geq1\),
\[
a(np^k)\equiv a(np^{k-1})\pmod {p^{3k}}.
\]
The proof will establish a somewhat stronger one-step assertion whose modulus depends on the \(p\)-adic order of the index.

Throughout, \(v_p(x)\) denotes the exponent of \(p\) in a positive integer \(x\). Whenever the argument below involves \(v_p(0)\), we may use the harmless convention \(v_p(0)=0\); every divisibility assertion involving a zero integer is automatic, and the zero cases will be separated where needed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Two sums over reduced residue classes
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We first record two elementary facts about sums modulo a prime power. Let \(s\geq1\). Since \(p\geq5\), both 2 and 3 are units modulo \(p^s\). We claim that
\[
\sum_{x\in(\mathbb Z/p^s\mathbb Z)^\times}x^{-1}=0,
\qquad
\sum_{x\in(\mathbb Z/p^s\mathbb Z)^\times}x^{-2}=0. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, multiplication by 2 permutes the units. Under that permutation, the first summand is multiplied by \(2^{-1}\). Thus, if its sum is \(S_1\), then
\[
S_1=2^{-1}S_1.
\]
The coefficient \(2^{-1}-1=-2^{-1}\) is a unit, so \(S_1=0\). Similarly, if the second sum is \(S_2\), then
\[
S_2=2^{-2}S_2.
\]
Now
\[
2^{-2}-1=(2^{-1}-1)(2^{-1}+1),
\]
and both factors are units: the first differs from a unit multiple of \(-1\), and the second is a unit multiple of 3. Hence \(S_2=0\), proving (1).

More generally, if \(p^s\mid N\), splitting \(0,1,\ldots,N-1\) into blocks of length \(p^s\) shows that, for any function \(g\) on the residue ring,
\[
\sum_{\substack{0\leq a<N\\p\nmid a}}g(a)
 =\frac N{p^s}\sum_{x\in(\mathbb Z/p^s\mathbb Z)^\times}g(x)
 \quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/p^s\mathbb Z. \tag{2}
\]
Here a residue is a unit modulo \(p^s\) exactly when it is not divisible by \(p\). Taking \(g(x)=x^{-1}\) and \(g(x)=x^{-2}\), (1) and (2) give
\[
\sum_{\substack{0\leq a<N\\p\nmid a}}a^{-1}=0,
\qquad
\sum_{\substack{0\leq a<N\\p\nmid a}}a^{-2}=0
\quad\pmod {p^s}. \tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Symmetric products of the numbers not divisible by \(p\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Fix \(L\geq0\), put \(M=Lp\), and let
\[
\mathcal A=\{a:0\leq a<M,\ p\nmid a\}.
\]
Suppose \(p^s\mid M\), with \(s\geq1\). Define
\[
E_1=\sum_{c\in\mathcal A}\prod_{a\in\mathcal A\setminus\{c\}}a,
\qquad
E_2=\sum_{\substack{T\subseteq\mathcal A\\|T|=2}}
          \prod_{a\in\mathcal A\setminus T}a.
\]
We need the divisibilities
\[
p^{2s}\mid E_1,\qquad p^s\mid E_2. \tag{4}
\]

Let \(D=\prod_{a\in\mathcal A}a\). Every member of \(\mathcal A\) is a unit modulo \(p^s\). Therefore, modulo \(p^s\),
\[
E_2=D\sum_{\substack{T\subseteq\mathcal A\\|T|=2}}
                 \prod_{a\in T}a^{-1}.
\]
For arbitrary numbers \(x_a\), expansion of a square gives
\[
\left(\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}x_a\right)^2
 =\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}x_a^2
  +2\sum_{\substack{T\subseteq\mathcal A\\|T|=2}}
        \prod_{a\in T}x_a.
\]
Take \(x_a=a^{-1}\). By (3), the first sum and the sum of squares are both zero modulo \(p^s\). Since 2 is invertible, the pair sum is zero modulo \(p^s\), and hence so is \(E_2\). This proves the second assertion in (4).

For \(E_1\), pair every \(c\in\mathcal A\) with \(M-c\). This is again in \(\mathcal A\), and it is different from \(c\). Indeed, equality would imply \(2c=M\); since \(p\mid M\) and \(p\neq2\), it would follow that \(p\mid c\), a contradiction. Put
\[
U=\sum_{c\in\mathcal A}
       \prod_{a\in\mathcal A\setminus\{c,M-c\}}a.
\]
Adding the terms indexed by \(c\) after reindexing by \(c\mapsto M-c\) gives the exact integer identity
\[
2E_1=MU. \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, the two omitted-factor products corresponding to \(c\) and \(M-c\) have sum
\[
((M-c)+c)\prod_{a\in\mathcal A\setminus\{c,M-c\}}a
 =M\prod_{a\in\mathcal A\setminus\{c,M-c\}}a.
\]
Modulo \(p^s\), we have \(M-c\equiv-c\). Consequently,
\[
\prod_{a\in\mathcal A\setminus\{c,M-c\}}a
 =D\,(c(M-c))^{-1}
 \equiv-Dc^{-2}\pmod {p^s}.
\]
By (3), \(U\equiv-D\sum c^{-2}\equiv0\pmod {p^s}\). Since also \(p^s\mid M\), (5) yields \(p^{2s}\mid2E_1\). The odd number \(p^{2s}\) is coprime to 2, so \(p^{2s}\mid E_1\). This completes (4).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. A shifted-product congruence
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(B,L\geq0\), and write
\[
v_B=v_p(B),\qquad v_L=v_p(L),\qquad w=\min(v_B,v_L).
\]
We claim
\[
p^{3+3w}\mid
 \prod_{\substack{0\leq a<Lp\\p\nmid a}}(Bp+a)
 -\prod_{\substack{0\leq a<Lp\\p\nmid a}}a. \tag{6}
\]
If \(B=0\), the difference is zero. Assume henceforth that \(B>0\). Put \(s=v_L+1\). If \(L>0\), then \(p^s\mid Lp\); if \(L=0\), both products are empty and (6) is again immediate.

For any finite set \(S\) and integer \(y\), expansion according to the subset of factors from which \(y\) is selected gives
\[
\prod_{a\in S}(y+a)
 =\sum_{r=0}^{|S|}y^r
   \sum_{\substack{T\subseteq S\\|T|=r}}
       \prod_{a\in S\setminus T}a. \tag{7}
\]
Apply this with \(S=\mathcal A\) and \(y=Bp\), and subtract the term for \(r=0\). Because \(p^{v_B+1}\mid Bp\), the term with \(r=1\), using (4), is divisible by
\[
p^{(v_B+1)+2(v_L+1)}.
\]
The term with \(r=2\) is divisible by
\[
p^{2(v_B+1)+(v_L+1)}.
\]
Every term with \(r\geq3\) is divisible by \(p^{3(v_B+1)}\). Each of the three displayed exponents is at least
\(3+3\min(v_B,v_L)\). Thus every term in the difference (7) is divisible by \(p^{3+3w}\), proving (6).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. A strengthened binomial congruence
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Define the product with the multiples of \(p\) removed by
\[
G_p(R)=\prod_{\substack{1\leq j\leq Rp\\p\nmid j}}j.
\]
Separating the multiples \(p,2p,\ldots,Rp\) from \((Rp)!\) gives
\[
(Rp)!=G_p(R)p^R R!. \tag{8}
\]
If \(0\leq B\leq A\), set \(L=A-B\). Applying (8) to the factorial formula for the binomial coefficient and cancelling the common positive factorial factors gives the exact identity
\[
\binom{Ap}{Bp}G_p(B)G_p(L)=\binom ABG_p(A). \tag{9}
\]
Also, splitting the defining product for \(G_p(B+L)\) after \(Bp\) gives
\[
G_p(A)=G_p(B)
 \prod_{\substack{0\leq a<Lp\\p\nmid a}}(Bp+a). \tag{10}
\]
The use of \(0\leq a<Lp\) rather than \(1\leq a\leq Lp\) makes no difference, because 0 is excluded and \(Lp\) is divisible by \(p\).

Set
\[
c=\binom{Ap}{Bp},\quad d=\binom AB,\quad
D=\prod_{\substack{0\leq a<Lp\\p\nmid a}}a,
\quad
P=\prod_{\substack{0\leq a<Lp\\p\nmid a}}(Bp+a).
\]
After substituting (10) into (9) and cancelling the nonzero factor \(G_p(B)\), we obtain
\[
cD=dP,
\]
and hence
\[
(c-d)D=d(P-D). \tag{11}
\]
The integer \(D\) is coprime to \(p\). By (6),
\[
p^{3+3\min(v_p(B),v_p(A-B))}\mid P-D,
\]
while by definition
\[
p^{v_p(\binom AB)}\mid d.
\]
Thus (11), followed by cancellation of the factor \(D\), which is coprime to the relevant power of \(p\), proves
\[
\boxed{
 p^{v_p(\binom AB)+3+3\min(v_p(B),v_p(A-B))}
 \mid \binom{Ap}{Bp}-\binom AB.} \tag{12}
\]
This remains true in the endpoint cases: when \(B=0\) or \(B=A\), the two binomial coefficients are both 1, so the difference vanishes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Two valuation inequalities
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For \(1\leq i\leq m\), the identity
\[
m\binom{m-1}{i-1}=i\binom mi
\]
implies, on taking \(p\)-adic orders,
\[
v_p(m)\leq v_p(i)+v_p\!\binom mi. \tag{13}
\]
Applying (13) to both \(x\) and \(y\) in \(x+y\), and using
\(\binom{x+y}{x}=\binom{x+y}{y}\), gives, for \(x,y\geq1\),
\[
v_p(x+y)
 \leq v_p\!\binom{x+y}{x}+\min(v_p(x),v_p(y)). \tag{14}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Congruence for one scaled multinomial summand
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(i+j\leq m\), and put
\[
\begin{aligned}
c_1&=\binom{mp}{ip},& d_1&=\binom mi,\\
c_2&=\binom{(m-i)p}{jp},& d_2&=\binom{m-i}{j},\\
C&=c_1c_2,&D&=d_1d_2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Let
\[
t=v_p(m),\quad v_1=v_p(d_1),\quad v_2=v_p(d_2),
\]
and
\[
w_1=\min(v_p(i),v_p(m-i)),\qquad
w_2=\min(v_p(j),v_p(m-i-j)).
\]
From (12),
\[
p^{v_1+3+3w_1}\mid c_1-d_1,
\qquad
p^{v_2+3+3w_2}\mid c_2-d_2. \tag{15}
\]
Also \(p^{v_1}\) divides both \(d_1\) and \(c_1\), and \(p^{v_2}\) divides both \(d_2\) and \(c_2\). Consequently,
\[
p^{v_1+v_2}\mid C,D,
\qquad p^{2(v_1+v_2)}\mid CD. \tag{16}
\]

We next relate \(t\) to the quantities in (15). If \(c_1-d_1\neq0\), then neither \(i=0\) nor \(i=m\), since in either endpoint case both binomial coefficients equal 1. Hence \(i,m-i\geq1\), and (14) gives
\[
t\leq v_1+w_1\leq v_1+v_2+w_1. \tag{17}
\]
Likewise, if \(c_2-d_2\neq0\), then \(j,m-i-j\geq1\), and (14) first gives
\[
v_p(m-i)\leq v_2+w_2.
\]
Furthermore,
\[
t\leq v_1+v_p(m-i). \tag{18}
\]
For \(i>0\), this is (14) applied to \(m=i+(m-i)\); for \(i=0\), it is immediate because \(d_1=1\) and \(m-i=m\). Combining these inequalities gives
\[
t\leq v_1+v_2+w_2. \tag{19}
\]

Now expand
\[
C-D=d_1(c_2-d_2)+d_2(c_1-d_1)
       +(c_1-d_1)(c_2-d_2). \tag{20}
\]
If either difference occurring here is zero, the corresponding term is zero. Otherwise, (15), (17), and (19) show term by term that
\[
p^{t+1}\mid C-D. \tag{21}
\]
For example, the first term has order at least
\(v_1+v_2+3+3w_2\), which is at least \(t+1\) by (19); the other two terms are handled similarly.

We need the cube, and use the identity
\[
C^3-D^3=(C-D)^3+3CD(C-D). \tag{22}
\]
The first term is divisible by \(p^{3(t+1)}\) by (21). For the second, insert the three-term expansion (20). From (16), each resulting term begins with order \(2(v_1+v_2)\). The term containing \(d_1(c_2-d_2)\) therefore has order at least
\[
2(v_1+v_2)+v_1+v_2+3+3w_2
 =3(v_1+v_2+w_2+1)\geq3(t+1)
\]
by (19). The term containing \(d_2(c_1-d_1)\) is treated using (17), and the product of the two differences has still larger order; if a difference is zero, the term vanishes. Thus
\[
\boxed{
p^{3(v_p(m)+1)}\mid
 \left(\binom{mp}{ip}\binom{(m-i)p}{jp}\right)^3
 -\left(\binom mi\binom{m-i}{j}\right)^3.} \tag{23}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Terms whose coordinates are not both divisible by \(p\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For \(r+s\leq mp\), define the multinomial coefficient
\[
Q=\binom{mp}{r}\binom{mp-r}{s}.
\]
If \(r,s\) are not both divisible by \(p\), then
\[
p^{v_p(m)+1}\mid Q. \tag{24}
\]
To see this, first note the symmetry
\[
\binom Nr\binom{N-r}{s}
 =\binom Ns\binom{N-s}{r}, \tag{25}
\]
which follows either from the factorial formula or by counting the same multinomial choices in the opposite order.

Let \(t=v_p(m)\). Since \(v_p(mp)=t+1\), if \(p\nmid r\), inequality (13) applied to \(\binom{mp}{r}\) gives
\[
t+1\leq v_p\!\binom{mp}{r},
\]
so (24) follows. If instead \(p\mid r\), then by hypothesis \(p\nmid s\), and after using (25), the same argument applies to \(\binom{mp}{s}\). Cubing (24) yields
\[
\boxed{p^{3(v_p(m)+1)}\mid
 \left(\binom{mp}{r}\binom{mp-r}{s}\right)^3} \tag{26}
\]
whenever \(r,s\) are not both divisible by \(p\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
8. The one-step supercongruence
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Write
\[
\mathcal D_N=\{(r,s)\in\mathbb N^2:r+s\leq N\}
\]
and
\[
T_N(r,s)=\left(\binom Nr\binom{N-r}{s}\right)^3.
\]
Then
\[
a(N)=\sum_{(r,s)\in\mathcal D_N}T_N(r,s).
\]
Split \(\mathcal D_{mp}\) into the pairs for which both coordinates are divisible by \(p\), and the remaining pairs. The first part is exactly the image of \(\mathcal D_m\) under
\((i,j)\mapsto(ip,jp)\): divisibility gives unique quotients, and
\(ip+jp\leq mp\) is equivalent to \(i+j\leq m\). Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(mp)-a(m)
={}&\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal D_m}
       \bigl(T_{mp}(ip,jp)-T_m(i,j)\bigr)\\
 &+\sum_{\substack{(r,s)\in\mathcal D_{mp}\\
                    \text{not both }r,s\text{ divisible by }p}}
       T_{mp}(r,s). \tag{27}
\end{aligned}
\]
Every summand in the first sum is divisible by \(p^{3(v_p(m)+1)}\) by (23), and every summand in the second sum is divisible by the same power by (26). Therefore
\[
\boxed{p^{3(v_p(m)+1)}\mid a(mp)-a(m)} \tag{28}
\]
for every positive \(m\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
9. Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Take
\[
m=np^{k-1}.
\]
It is positive because \(n\geq1\), and
\[
mp=np^k.
\]
Moreover,
\[
v_p(m)=v_p(n)+k-1\geq k-1.
\]
Thus
\[
3k\leq3(v_p(m)+1).
\]
By (28), \(p^{3(v_p(m)+1)}\) divides
\(a(np^k)-a(np^{k-1})\), and hence so does \(p^{3k}\). Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{a(np^k)\equiv a(np^{k-1})\pmod {p^{3k}}}.
\]
This proves the conjectured supercongruence for every prime \(p\geq5\) and all positive integers \(n,k\).
